basic_information.name: Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) & Agent Communication Protocol (ACP)
basic_information.creator: A2A: Google (announced April 9, 2025 at Google Cloud Next; donated to Linux Foundation June 23, 2025). ACP: IBM Research (announced March 2025; built for BeeAI platform; donated to Linux Foundation March 2025 under LF AI & Data). ACP merged into A2A under Linux Foundation governance in August-September 2025.
basic_information.release_date: A2A: April 9, 2025 (initial public specification). ACP: March 2025 (launched with BeeAI platform). Merger announced: August 29, 2025 (ACP joins forces with A2A under LF AI & Data).
basic_information.license: Apache License 2.0 (both A2A and ACP). The A2A specification and all official SDKs are open-source under Apache 2.0.
basic_information.current_version: A2A: v0.3.0 (released July 31, 2025 — added gRPC support, signed security cards, extended Python SDK). Draft v1.0 specification in development. ACP: effectively merged into A2A; final ACP version superseded by A2A v0.3+. Migration paths and documentation provided for ACP-to-A2A transition.

technical_architecture.architecture_pattern: protocol | multi_agent — A2A is an open protocol specification for agent-to-agent communication, not a framework or runtime. The architecture is organized in three layers: Layer 1 (transport) handles HTTP/gRPC connectivity, Layer 2 (abstract operations) defines fundamental capabilities and behaviors agents must support independent of transport, Layer 3 (protocol bindings) maps abstract operations to specific transports (JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC, HTTP+JSON). Core architectural principle is 'opaque execution' — agents collaborate without revealing internal logic, memory, or tool implementations, preserving data privacy and intellectual property. ACP used a simpler REST-based approach with HTTP endpoints for sending, receiving, and routing messages.
technical_architecture.underlying_models: Model-agnostic by design. A2A is a protocol, not tied to any specific LLM. Compatible with agents built on any framework or model. Supported by agent frameworks including: Google Agent Development Kit (ADK, native A2A support), LangChain/LangGraph (A2A endpoint support), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (A2A protocol contract), Microsoft Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, Spring AI (A2A integration since January 2026), CrewAI, and virtually any HTTP-capable agent. SDKs available in Python, Java, Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, and C#/.NET.
technical_architecture.tool_integration: A2A is complementary to tool integration protocols like MCP — A2A handles agent-to-agent communication (horizontal), while MCP handles agent-to-tool communication (vertical). A2A does not prescribe how agents connect to tools internally. Instead, each agent uses its own tool integration mechanism (MCP, function calling, plugins, etc.) and exposes capabilities to other agents via A2A Agent Cards. The Agent Card advertises 'skills' — high-level capability descriptions that abstract away internal tool implementations. ACP had a similar approach with metadata-based agent manifests.
technical_architecture.planning_approach: Not applicable — A2A is a communication protocol, not a planning system. Planning is handled by each individual agent or its underlying framework. A2A's contribution to planning is enabling distributed task delegation: a client agent can discover remote agents' capabilities via Agent Cards, delegate subtasks based on skill matching, and coordinate task completion across multiple agents. The protocol supports task lifecycle management (submitted, working, input-required, completed, failed, canceled, rejected) that enables planning systems to track distributed work.
technical_architecture.multi_agent_support: A2A IS the multi-agent interoperability protocol. Core multi-agent patterns supported: (1) Client-Server — one agent (client) delegates tasks to another agent (server) discovered via Agent Cards, (2) Orchestration — a coordinating agent dispatches subtasks to multiple specialized agents, (3) Peer-to-peer — agents communicate bidirectionally using push notifications and streaming, (4) Human-in-the-loop — agents can request human input via the 'input-required' task state. Sessions group related tasks for contextual continuity. The protocol is designed to work across framework boundaries — a LangGraph agent can communicate with a Google ADK agent via A2A without either knowing the other's implementation.

memory_and_context.memory_types_supported: none (protocol-level) — A2A is a stateless communication protocol; it does not manage agent memory itself. However, A2A supports stateful interactions through Sessions: a session groups related tasks and enables contextual continuity between a client and server agent. The session mechanism allows agents to maintain conversational context across multiple task exchanges. Actual memory management (short-term, episodic, semantic) is the responsibility of each agent's underlying framework, not the A2A protocol.
memory_and_context.context_window_management: Not applicable at protocol level. A2A uses a structured message format with 'Parts' (TextPart, FilePart, DataPart) that carry content between agents. The protocol does not manage LLM context windows directly. Each agent is responsible for managing its own context. The opaque execution model means agents can internally use any context strategy (truncation, summarization, RAG) without exposing it to peer agents.
memory_and_context.persistence_mechanism: in_memory | implementation-dependent — The A2A protocol defines Tasks with unique IDs and lifecycle states that can be persisted. Sessions provide logical grouping of related tasks. The protocol specification does not mandate a specific persistence mechanism — implementations can use in-memory stores, databases, or cloud storage. Push notifications enable disconnected operation where task state changes are delivered to webhook URLs, reducing the need for persistent connections.
memory_and_context.context_engineering_approach: A2A addresses context sharing between agents through structured message Parts: TextPart (plain text), FilePart (files with inline bytes or URI references), and DataPart (structured JSON data). Artifacts serve as task outputs that carry rich content between agents. Agent Cards provide declarative context about agent capabilities, enabling informed delegation decisions. The protocol treats inter-agent context as a first-class concern — agents exchange context through well-defined message structures rather than sharing raw internal state.

capabilities.core_capabilities: Open protocol for secure agent-to-agent communication and interoperability across frameworks, vendors, and platforms. Key capabilities: (1) Agent Discovery — agents publish Agent Cards (JSON metadata documents) at /.well-known/agent-card.json describing identity, capabilities, skills, endpoints, and authentication requirements. (2) Task Management — tasks are the fundamental unit of work with a defined lifecycle (submitted, working, input-required, completed, failed, canceled, rejected). Tasks support immediate completion or long-running asynchronous execution. (3) Flexible Interaction Modes — synchronous request/response, streaming via Server-Sent Events (SSE), and asynchronous push notifications via webhooks. (4) Structured Messaging — messages contain Parts (TextPart, FilePart, DataPart) for multimodal content exchange. (5) Session Management — sessions group related tasks for contextual continuity. (6) Artifacts — structured task outputs that carry results between agents. (7) Multiple Protocol Bindings — JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON (v0.3+). (8) Enterprise-Grade Security — OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, API keys, signed Agent Cards for cryptographic identity verification. (9) Observability — native OpenTelemetry support with W3C Trace Context propagation for distributed tracing.
capabilities.supported_modalities: Text (TextPart), files (FilePart with inline bytes or URI references), structured data (DataPart as JSON objects). The protocol is modality-agnostic at the transport level — actual modality support depends on the agents communicating. Agents can exchange any content type through Parts. The FilePart type supports arbitrary MIME types enabling image, audio, video, and document exchange.
capabilities.autonomy_level: Not applicable — A2A is a protocol, not an agent. The protocol supports any autonomy level from supervised to fully autonomous. The 'input-required' task state enables human-in-the-loop patterns where agents pause execution and wait for human input. The protocol's security model (authentication, authorization, signed cards) supports enterprise oversight requirements. Autonomy decisions are made by the agents and their deployment configurations.
capabilities.tool_ecosystem: A2A is not a tool protocol — it is an agent communication protocol. However, it creates an ecosystem of interoperable agents that function as 'tools' for each other. Over 150 organizations support A2A as of mid-2025. Major platform integrations: Google ADK (native A2A), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (A2A protocol contract), LangChain/LangGraph (A2A endpoint), Spring AI (A2A integration), Microsoft Semantic Kernel. The a2a-samples repository provides reference implementations. The awesome-a2a community repository tracks A2A-compatible agents and tools.

agent_interoperability.mcp_support: A2A and MCP (Model Context Protocol) are complementary, not competing. A2A handles agent-to-agent communication (horizontal); MCP handles agent-to-tool/data communication (vertical). A practical enterprise architecture layers both: MCP for individual agent tool access, A2A for multi-agent coordination. Example: an inventory agent uses MCP to query a database, then uses A2A to communicate with an external supplier agent. Both protocols are now under Linux Foundation governance (A2A under LF AI & Data, MCP under AAIF).
agent_interoperability.a2a_support: A2A IS the Agent-to-Agent protocol. It defines the standard for agent-to-agent interoperability. All A2A-compatible agents can communicate regardless of underlying framework, vendor, or platform. The protocol achieves interoperability through: standardized Agent Cards for capability discovery, JSON-RPC/gRPC/HTTP bindings for transport, structured message format for content exchange, and task lifecycle for workflow coordination.
agent_interoperability.agents_md_support: AGENTS.md is a separate standard under the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) contributed by OpenAI. A2A and AGENTS.md address different concerns: AGENTS.md provides project-specific instructions for coding agents, while A2A provides the communication protocol between agents. They can coexist — an agent reading AGENTS.md for project context can use A2A for inter-agent communication.
agent_interoperability.cross_framework_compatibility: Extremely high — cross-framework interoperability is A2A's core purpose. Supported by: Google (ADK, Vertex AI), Microsoft (Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, Azure AI Foundry), Amazon (Bedrock AgentCore), Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, Cisco, LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, Spring AI (Java ecosystem), Quarkus (gRPC support). SDKs in 5+ languages (Python, Java, Go, JavaScript, .NET) ensure framework-agnostic adoption. The protocol's use of standard HTTP/JSON-RPC means any HTTP-capable system can participate. Over 150 organizations support A2A, including technology companies, system integrators (Accenture, Deloitte, McKinsey, PwC), and enterprise software vendors.

safety_and_guardrails.permission_model: capability_based — A2A's security model treats agents as standard enterprise applications. Authentication is managed at the HTTP transport layer, not within message payloads. Agent Cards advertise supported authentication schemes aligned with OpenAPI specification: API keys, OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect Discovery. Authorization is implementation-specific: servers authorize requests based on authenticated identity (end user, client application, or both). Access can be controlled per-skill using OAuth scopes. Version 0.3 introduced signed Agent Cards for cryptographic identity verification, critical for enterprise deployments where agents must prove their identity.
safety_and_guardrails.escalation_policy: The A2A protocol supports escalation through the 'input-required' task state. When a remote agent needs human input or additional authorization, it transitions the task to input-required, signaling the client to obtain necessary information. Push notifications deliver state changes (including escalation events) to client webhook URLs. The protocol does not prescribe specific escalation policies — these are implemented by the agents and their deployment environments. Enterprise deployments can integrate A2A with existing IAM and policy management systems.
safety_and_guardrails.hallucination_mitigation: Not directly addressed at protocol level — A2A is a communication protocol, not an inference system. However, A2A's structured communication (typed Parts, defined task states, Agent Card capabilities) reduces the risk of miscommunication between agents. The opaque execution model means each agent is responsible for its own hallucination mitigation internally. The protocol's audit trail capabilities enable post-hoc detection of agent errors across distributed workflows.
safety_and_guardrails.audit_trail: Yes — A2A provides comprehensive audit trail support. All communication uses structured JSON-RPC/gRPC messages that are fully loggable. Each task has a unique taskId, sessions have sessionIds, and correlation IDs enable tracing across agent interactions. OpenTelemetry integration propagates trace context (W3C Trace Context headers) across agent boundaries. Servers expose metrics (request rates, error rates, latency). Enterprise deployments can feed A2A logs into SIEM platforms for security monitoring and compliance auditing.
safety_and_guardrails.human_oversight_pattern: pre-approval | confidence_threshold — The 'input-required' task state enables agents to pause and request human input at any point. Agent Cards can declare which skills require human authorization via OAuth scopes. The protocol supports the full oversight spectrum from fully autonomous (task completes without human interaction) to always-on human approval (every task requires input). Push notifications enable asynchronous human review of long-running tasks. The choice of oversight pattern is left to the deployment, not prescribed by the protocol.

governance_and_standards.governance_body: Linux Foundation AI & Data (LF AI & Data). A2A was donated by Google to the Linux Foundation and officially launched as a hosted project on June 23, 2025 at Open Source Summit North America. Governed by a Technical Steering Committee (TSC) with representatives from Google, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Cisco, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and SAP. IBM's Kate Blair joined the TSC when ACP merged into A2A. Separately, the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF, formed December 9, 2025) governs complementary projects (MCP, AGENTS.md, goose). Both A2A and AAIF are under the Linux Foundation umbrella, representing the two pillars of agent interoperability: agent-to-agent (A2A) and agent-to-tool (MCP/AAIF).
governance_and_standards.contributing_protocols: A2A is the protocol. It incorporates and merges IBM's Agent Communication Protocol (ACP) which brought REST-native patterns, metadata-based agent discovery, and BeeAI platform expertise. A2A builds on established standards: JSON-RPC 2.0 (wire format), gRPC (high-performance RPC), HTTP/HTTPS (transport), Server-Sent Events (streaming), OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (authentication), W3C Trace Context (distributed tracing), OpenTelemetry (observability). The protocol is designed to complement MCP (agent-to-tool) — together they form the complete agent interoperability stack.
governance_and_standards.regulatory_compliance: No direct regulatory compliance certifications for the protocol specification itself — A2A is an open standard, not a deployed service. Compliance depends on implementation. The protocol supports enterprise compliance requirements through: enterprise-grade authentication (OAuth 2.0, OIDC), signed Agent Cards for cryptographic identity, comprehensive audit trails via OpenTelemetry, HTTPS-only communication requirement in production, integration with existing IAM and SIEM systems. The protocol's design aligns with enterprise security frameworks but does not itself certify EU AI Act, SOC2, or HIPAA compliance. Implementations must handle GDPR and data sovereignty requirements at the application layer. [uncertain]

deployment_and_operations.deployment_modes: cloud | local | hybrid | edge — A2A is transport-agnostic and can be deployed anywhere HTTP/gRPC is available. (1) Cloud: agents deployed as microservices on Kubernetes, Cloud Run, ECS, or serverless functions. (2) Local: agents running as local processes communicating over localhost. (3) Hybrid: mix of cloud-hosted and on-premises agents communicating via A2A. (4) Edge: lightweight agents at the edge communicating with cloud-hosted agents. The protocol's use of standard HTTP/gRPC means it works with existing infrastructure: load balancers, API gateways, service meshes, CDNs.
deployment_and_operations.scalability_model: horizontal | serverless — Each A2A agent is an independent service that scales independently. Horizontal scaling via container orchestration (Kubernetes). Serverless deployment possible for lightweight agents (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run). The protocol supports both stateful (session-based) and stateless operation, enabling scaling decisions per agent. Push notifications decouple client-server timing, reducing connection overhead. gRPC support (v0.3) provides higher throughput for performance-critical deployments.
deployment_and_operations.cost_per_task: The protocol itself is free (open-source, Apache 2.0). Infrastructure costs depend on deployment: (1) Agent hosting: standard compute costs for HTTP/gRPC services, (2) Serverless: pay-per-invocation pricing, (3) The dominant cost in A2A-based systems is the LLM inference cost for each participating agent, not the protocol overhead. A2A adds minimal network overhead — messages are compact JSON-RPC/gRPC payloads. Enterprise costs include agent infrastructure, monitoring, and security layers. [uncertain]
deployment_and_operations.resource_requirements: Lightweight for the protocol layer. A2A agents are standard HTTP/gRPC services with minimal protocol overhead. Requirements depend on the agent's underlying framework and model: (1) Minimum: any system capable of serving HTTP requests (even a Raspberry Pi for simple agents), (2) Typical cloud deployment: standard container resources (256Mi-1Gi memory, 0.5-2 CPU cores per agent instance), (3) Full enterprise deployment with monitoring: multi-instance agents behind load balancers, OpenTelemetry collector, log aggregation. No special hardware required for the protocol itself. GPU requirements depend on whether agents run local LLM inference.

observability_and_ops.monitoring_integration: A2A natively supports OpenTelemetry for monitoring and observability. The protocol propagates trace context (W3C Trace Context headers) across agent boundaries enabling end-to-end visibility. A2A servers should expose operational metrics: request rates, error rates, task processing latency, and resource utilization. Compatible with standard monitoring stacks: Prometheus + Grafana for metrics, Jaeger for distributed tracing, ELK/Splunk for log aggregation. Enterprise SIEM integration supported through structured logging. The protocol's reliance on HTTP allows integration with existing API monitoring tools (Datadog, New Relic, etc.).
observability_and_ops.tracing_support: Yes — first-class distributed tracing support. OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) format for structured logs and metrics. W3C Trace Context headers propagated across agent interactions. Each request/response carries trace IDs and span IDs enabling debugging across multi-agent workflows. Task IDs, session IDs, and correlation IDs provide additional tracing dimensions. Comprehensive logging includes details on both client and server sides for troubleshooting and auditing.
observability_and_ops.production_readiness_level: beta — A2A v0.3.0 is the current stable release, with the team committed to backward compatibility starting at v0.3. Draft v1.0 specification is in development. Major enterprise platforms have A2A support (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Google ADK, LangChain), indicating real production use. However, the protocol is still pre-1.0 and evolving. Over 150 organizations support A2A, and Fortune 500 companies are evaluating deployment. Full production-ready v1.0 release is anticipated for late 2025 or early 2026.

ACP repo (i-am-bee/acp): 935 stars, 113 forks. awesome-a2a community repo: ~500 stars. A2A Python SDK, Java SDK, Go SDK, JS SDK maintained as separate repos under a2aproject organization.
adoption_and_market.adoption_scale: 150+ supporting organizations as of mid-2025. Major technology partners: Google, Microsoft, Amazon (AWS), Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, Cisco, Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, LangChain, MongoDB, PayPal, UKG, Workday. Leading service providers: Accenture, BCG, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte, HCLTech, Infosys, KPMG, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, Wipro. Framework integrations: Google ADK (native), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, LangChain/LangGraph, Spring AI, Quarkus, Microsoft Semantic Kernel. SDKs downloaded across 5 languages. Growing developer community on GitHub with active discussions and contributions.
adoption_and_market.pricing_model: open-source — The protocol specification, all SDKs, and reference implementations are completely free under Apache 2.0 license. No licensing fees. Revenue opportunities exist for: A2A-compatible agent hosting platforms, enterprise A2A gateway products, consulting and integration services, and A2A-native SaaS products.
adoption_and_market.key_use_cases: Enterprise multi-agent orchestration across vendor boundaries. Supply chain automation (inventory agent communicates with supplier agents). Customer service escalation (tier-1 bot delegates to specialized agents). Financial services (compliance agent coordinates with fraud detection, KYC, and reporting agents). Healthcare (scheduling agent communicates with insurance verification and patient record agents). Retail (purchase concierge agent interacts with seller agents — as shown in Google Codelabs tutorial). Cross-organization agent collaboration where agents from different companies need to interoperate securely. IT operations (monitoring agent delegates remediation to specialized ops agents).
adoption_and_market.competitive_position: Dominant position for agent-to-agent interoperability. A2A has effectively won the agent communication protocol race by absorbing its main competitor (IBM's ACP) and securing backing from every major cloud provider (Google, Microsoft, AWS) and enterprise software vendor. The only potential alternative is the Agentic AI Foundation's broader ecosystem, but AAIF and A2A are complementary rather than competing (AAIF focuses on MCP/tools, A2A on inter-agent communication). Both are under the Linux Foundation umbrella. A2A's early mover advantage, broad industry coalition, and absorption of ACP make it the de facto standard. No significant challenger exists as of early 2026.

human_agent_interaction.autonomy_spectrum: Not applicable as a protocol — A2A provides infrastructure for any autonomy level. The 'input-required' task state enables human-in-the-loop interactions. Agent Cards can declare skill-level authorization requirements. The protocol supports the full spectrum: (1) Fully autonomous task completion, (2) Human approval at task boundaries, (3) Continuous human oversight via streaming updates, (4) Human-initiated delegation to agent teams.
human_agent_interaction.handoff_mechanism: A2A defines handoff through task state transitions. When a server agent cannot complete a task, it can: (1) Transition to 'input-required' to request more information from the client (which may involve a human), (2) Transition to 'failed' with error details enabling the client to try an alternative agent, (3) Use push notifications to alert the client of state changes asynchronously. The client agent can then reassign the task to a different remote agent discovered via Agent Cards. The protocol also supports multi-turn conversations within a session for iterative human-agent-agent interactions.
human_agent_interaction.feedback_loop: Not directly implemented at protocol level. A2A enables feedback loops indirectly: (1) Task outcomes (completed, failed) provide signal about agent reliability, (2) Agent Cards can be updated to reflect improved capabilities, (3) Session history provides context for evaluating multi-turn interactions, (4) OpenTelemetry metrics enable performance-based routing (preferring faster or more reliable agents). Actual feedback-to-improvement loops are implemented at the application or orchestration layer, not prescribed by the protocol.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Important infrastructure knowledge for startups building multi-agent AI systems. USE A2A WHEN: (1) Building a product that coordinates multiple AI agents across different vendors or frameworks — A2A is the emerging standard, (2) Creating an AI agent that other companies' agents need to call — publish an Agent Card so you are discoverable, (3) Building cross-organizational agent workflows (e.g., supply chain, financial services, healthcare) where agents from different companies must interoperate securely, (4) Need vendor-neutral agent communication — avoid lock-in to a single cloud provider's agent ecosystem. AVOID/WAIT WHEN: (1) Building a single-agent product — A2A adds unnecessary complexity; use MCP for tool connectivity instead, (2) All your agents are within one framework (e.g., all LangGraph) — use the framework's native multi-agent patterns first, (3) Need agent-to-tool connectivity — use MCP, not A2A, (4) Your product does not involve inter-agent communication at all. STARTUP OPPORTUNITY: A2A creates opportunities for: A2A gateway/security products (authentication, audit, rate limiting for agent-to-agent traffic), agent marketplace platforms (Agent Card directories), cross-enterprise agent orchestration platforms, and A2A-native SaaS agents that advertise capabilities to other agents. The merger of ACP into A2A signals consolidation — building on A2A is a safe bet for interoperability.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy: The protocol and SDKs are free (Apache 2.0) — no buy decision for the protocol itself. Key decisions: (1) IMPLEMENT A2A when you need your agents to be discoverable and callable by external agents or when building multi-vendor agent workflows, (2) USE an A2A-compatible framework (Google ADK, LangGraph, Bedrock AgentCore) rather than implementing A2A from scratch — SDKs handle the protocol details, (3) BUILD custom Agent Cards and skills when you have unique capabilities to offer, (4) BUY/USE enterprise A2A security layers (API gateways, auth providers like Auth0) rather than implementing your own agent authentication. Cost: implementing basic A2A support using an SDK takes 1-3 days of developer time; using a framework with native A2A support (Google ADK) takes hours.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 3 (AI project framing) — A2A as interoperability decision in multi-agent architecture design, understanding when A2A is needed vs. simpler patterns. Session 4 (AI business models & strategy) — A2A as platform strategy enabling cross-vendor agent ecosystems, marketplace opportunities from Agent Card discovery, revenue models for A2A-native services. Session 5 (ethics and governance) — A2A governance as example of open-standard collaboration (Google, Microsoft, AWS, IBM under Linux Foundation), security implications of agent-to-agent communication, audit trail requirements for enterprise compliance.

confidence.caveats: A2A is still pre-1.0 — the specification is evolving and breaking changes may occur (v0.3 already changed the Agent Card well-known path). The claimed '150+ organizations' includes signatories of support, not necessarily production deployers. Production deployment data is limited — most enterprises are in evaluation or pilot phase as of early 2026. The A2A vs. AAIF relationship is still settling — while both are under the Linux Foundation, the governance boundary between them may shift. ACP migration to A2A may not be complete for all ACP users. GitHub star counts are approximate and growing. The competitive landscape could shift if a major player introduces an alternative protocol. Draft v1.0 timeline is uncertain — original expectation of late 2025 has not been met.
